Davies admitted on Swansea's website that, although he hadn't intended to leave, the opportunity was too good to pass up.

Mercedes-Benz faced scrutiny in Jiangsu, where the pricing authority discovered the German automaker pressured local dealerships to uphold price floors on select models, resulting in fines of 7.7 million yuan for some dealers. A Mercedes-Benz representative acknowledged the ruling, reiterated the company's commitment to competition laws, and mentioned steps taken to ensure full legal compliance. According to the Chinese regulator, Mercedes-Benz and its Jiangsu dealerships engaged in monopolistic practices by fixing minimum prices for E-Class and S-Class cars, as well as certain spare parts. Previously, Xinhua reported that Mercedes-Benz was also sanctioned for price manipulation in after-sales services in China, the world's largest market for international carmakers.

The future funding of S4C, primarily derived from the television license fee, is under scrutiny as the UK government comprehensively assesses the BBC. David Davies, MP for Monmouth, acknowledged to BBC Wales that S4C warrants "special" consideration due to its role in promoting the Welsh language. Despite this, government officials have suggested S4C should implement similar austerity measures as the BBC. The Labour party expressed apprehension on Thursday that BBC budget cuts could jeopardize S4C's financial stability. Culture Secretary John Whittingdale has reassured MPs of his dedication to the channel "within the next couple of years" and intends to engage in discussions with S4C's executives soon. Speaking on BBC Radio Cymru, Mr. Davies stated that the government understands S4C's significance and views it as crucial for the survival of the Welsh language. He also mentioned the potential for the Welsh Affairs Committee, which he leads, to investigate broadcasting matters, including S4C.

In August 1974, a body was discovered in Cockley Cley, near Swaffham, Norfolk, and Norfolk Police are now employing advanced methods for a subsequent post-mortem examination. Det Ch Insp Andy Guy stated that DNA retrieved from the remains could connect the woman to a surviving relative. The initial post-mortem, conducted on the day of the discovery on a heath, estimated her age to be between 23 and 35. She was found wearing a pink 1969 Marks & Spencer nightdress and wrapped in a plastic sheet tied with rope. Investigators are primarily focusing on the possibility that she was "The Duchess," a Great Yarmouth escort who detectives believe was originally from Denmark and vanished unexpectedly after being well-known in the area.

This research explored how environmental stress affects mate selection by comparing male army cadets in strenuous training to a control group, examining their attraction to varying female body types. Results showed that men in the demanding training environment preferred women with larger body sizes. Dr. Carlota Batres, the study's lead, suggested this shift is an adaptive mechanism, favoring partners seen as more robust and fertile in difficult circumstances. She highlighted that mate preferences are flexible and responsive to environmental signals, with the observed shift lasting as long as the stressful environment persisted. Dr. Batres theorized that such adaptations could be advantageous, improving the likelihood of pairing with individuals better able to withstand illness or resource scarcity. Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Perfecto Yasay plans to address the South China Sea issue at the Asia-Europe Meeting (Asem) summit, a two-day event beginning Friday in Ulaanbaatar with Chinese Premier Li Keqiang in attendance. This marks the first significant multilateral diplomatic forum following Tuesday's UN tribunal ruling, which invalidated China's broad claims in the region—a decision China has rejected, asserting the tribunal's lack of jurisdiction and reaffirming its continued operations. The Asem summit will convene 53 leaders from Asia and Europe, including delegates from Vietnam and Malaysia, both countries with rival claims in the South China Sea. The summit also represents the inaugural international conference for the new Philippine government.

Following a collision on the A9 involving a car with three children, 46-year-old articulated lorry driver John McCormack continued driving for 30 miles, Perth Sheriff Court heard. McCormack's conduct led to a two-year driving disqualification and a requirement to complete 250 hours of community service. According to Prosecutor Rebecca Kynaston, drivers traveling north near the House of Bruar shopping center had previously witnessed McCormack's lorry driving on the incorrect side of the road, causing them to veer onto the shoulder to avert crashes. Ignoring these close calls, the lorry then sideswiped a car occupied by a couple and their three children.

Kim Little of Seattle Reign secured the BBC World Service award, becoming its second recipient through a public vote. She surpassed Gaelle Enganamouit (FC Rosengard), Amandine Henry (Olympique Lyonnais), Carli Lloyd (Houston Dash), and Becky Sauerbrunn (FC Kansas City) for the honor. The 25-year-old Little expressed both surprise and appreciation upon receiving the award, emphasizing her hope for the continued progress of women's football. The award was presented to her at her team's training ground on Tuesday. Mary Hockaday, Head of BBC World Service English, commended Little and recognized the importance of the year for women's football. Hockaday also highlighted the BBC World Service's dedication to recognizing female football talent. Little stood out as Seattle's best player.

Stafford Hospital was plagued by allegations of serious neglect, including claims of patients resorting to drinking from flower vases and unqualified receptionists evaluating emergency situations. Julie Bailey, founder of Cure the NHS after her mother's experience, was awarded a CBE for her advocacy. Helene Donnelly, an A&E nurse who exposed the issues, received an OBE. Data showed a significantly elevated mortality rate at the hospital between 2005 and 2008. Distressed patients allegedly faced long waits, were denied pain relief, and sometimes lacked basic necessities like food and drink. Donnelly, who filed almost 100 complaints and testified at the public inquiry, expressed immense pride and honor in receiving an OBE for her NHS service, while acknowledging the challenges she had faced.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) determined that credit card companies had little motivation to assist customers in long-term debt due to the profitability of these accounts. Consequently, the FCA advocated for measures to encourage customers to increase their debt repayments. This investigation analyzed five years' worth of data from 34 million credit card holders and incorporated feedback from 40,000 interviews. Initial findings from the FCA revealed inconsistent competition, with some customers and products not receiving tailored assistance. Credit card providers were quick to assist customers falling behind on payments due to the "extreme unprofitability" they represented, a proactive approach not extended to those only making minimum payments. Joanna Elson, head of the Money Advice Trust, which operates National Debtline, shared the FCA's concern regarding the 1.6 million individuals struggling to manage their finances by making minimum payments, often across multiple cards, while also acknowledging credit card firms' general ability to support customers effectively.

Alex Brazier, the Bank of England's financial stability director, pointed out that unsecured household debt – including car loans, credit card balance transfers, and personal loans – is growing at an alarming rate of 10% per year, far exceeding the 1.5% increase in household incomes. Speaking at the University of Liverpool, Brazier cautioned that this surge in household debt poses a threat to borrowers, lenders, and the stability of the entire economy. He also warned that High Street banks are in danger of becoming overly complacent about this growing consumer debt, potentially leading to a swift decline in lending standards. David Dallimore, a Bangor University specialist in childcare and early childhood development, is advocating for significant changes to the education of three- and four-year-olds. Speaking on BBC's Eye on Wales, he contended that Wales lacks a consistent, enduring plan for early years assistance. The Welsh government has suggested it will contemplate reforms after examining the specifics of the forthcoming Childcare Bill. At present, all children in this age group are guaranteed at least 10 hours of education through the Foundation Phase. Nevertheless, each of Wales' 22 local councils independently administers the distribution of these hours for three-year-olds and determines funding levels. This decentralized approach has produced substantial differences in service quality and adaptability across the nation, leading to a fragmented and inconsistent system.

Taking the 13 engines out of service, as they haven't been used for two years, would leave London with 142 operational vehicles and free up funds to hire more firefighters for Fire Rescue Units. However, the Fire Brigades Union (FBU) argues that permanently removing these engines would be "dangerous and reckless." The London Fire Brigade (LFB) has suggested three ways to cut costs, promising no station closures or job losses. The LFB insists it has met city-wide response time goals even without the 13 engines, claiming their return would only shave about four seconds off the first engine's arrival time. London Assembly Member Andrew Dismore has put forward a different plan.

Dee Stitt, a prominent UDA figure associated with Charter NI, faced backlash for comments he made in a Guardian interview. Charter NI's board issued a statement conveying "deep disappointment and great concern" regarding the article and pledged an internal review. In the interview, Stitt referred to the North Down Defenders loyalist band as "our homeland security" and claimed governmental neglect of Northern Ireland. Charter NI, a community organization, had been awarded a Â£1.7 million grant from the Northern Ireland Executive's social investment fund. SDLP MLA Nichola Mallon insisted that Stitt's position as Charter NI's CEO was unsustainable, calling for his immediate resignation and noting that Charter NI's statement confirmed his continued role as CEO.

PC Frances Tilley confessed that her career with Northamptonshire Police was finished after she avoided paying for a train ride from Bristol Temple Meads to Castle Cary in Somerset last June. The disciplinary hearing at police headquarters revealed that Tilley, a probationary officer with under two years on the job, was dismissed for gross misconduct. The hearing at Wootton Hall centered on Tilley's trip from Northampton to Castle Cary on June 22nd of the previous year. Despite being described as "diligent, professional and committed," she failed to buy a ticket for the last portion of her journey while traveling with others. Force solicitor Elizabeth Briggs explained that Tilley traveled without a ticket from Bristol to Westbury and then to Castle Cary, despite having several chances to purchase one.

A jewelry exhibition at the Carlton Hotel in Cannes, located on the Croisette, was robbed on Sunday morning. This theft is the most significant in a string of notable robberies in Cannes, a city renowned for its film festival. Interestingly, the Carlton Hotel served as the backdrop for Alfred Hitchcock's 1955 movie "To Catch A Thief," about a jewel thief operating on the French Riviera. The hotel lobby was hosting a Leviev diamond exhibition when the robbery occurred. According to local news, the thief escaped with the jewels in a briefcase, and the owner remains unidentified. A Cannes police spokesperson indicated that, if the estimated value of the stolen jewels proves accurate, this would be the second-largest jewelry heist ever in France.

Tottenham Hotspur is playing its Champions League home games at Wembley Stadium while White Hart Lane is being rebuilt. However, their recent 1-0 defeat on Wednesday was their second European loss at the national stadium this season. Despite this, manager Pochettino defended Wembley, stating there's "nowhere better in the world to play football," blaming the losses on the team's substandard performance. Faced with the prospect of using Wembley for all home games next season, Pochettino expressed his disappointment with their performances, particularly against Monaco and Bayer Leverkusen. He emphasized the importance of addressing internal issues and lamented the team's failure to meet its usual performance level. This loss to Leverkusen follows their earlier 2-1 defeat to Monaco at Wembley in their first Champions League match.

During a BBC debate at the University of Lincoln before the EU referendum, a neutral panelist expressed frustration at being "battered on both sides by half-truths, lies and scaremongering." The debate, set to air on Sunday, featured UKIP MEP Jane Collins (for Leave), Labour MP Melanie Onn (for Remain), and journalist Robin Limb. A key dispute centered on the EU's effect on the NHS. Collins, representing Yorkshire and Humber, criticized the UK's £675 million annual contribution to EU health schemes versus the £49 million received as "an atrocity," advocating for Brexit to benefit the NHS. She also suggested simplifying nurse qualification processes and guaranteeing fair compensation for all NHS personnel. Onn, the MP for Great Grimsby, countered by:

Last year, Wolverhampton hotel owner Ranjit Singh Power vanished during a business trip to Punjab. While a taxi driver admitted to the murder, BBC India Correspondent Sanjoy Majumder suggests local police suspect additional individuals were involved. Power's family urgently seeks to learn the full story behind his disappearance and expresses frustration over the absence of information from the Foreign Office and Indian officials. His brother, Amrik Singh Power, recounts their relentless pursuit of answers, emphasizing his numerous attempts to get updates from the Foreign Office. Mr. Power was last seen on May 8th at an Amritsar, Punjab airport, and his family reported him missing following a week without contact. The taxi driver, Sukhdev Singh, who

In July, the University of Birmingham announced the unearthing of a 1,370-year-old Quran manuscript, hailed as "a global treasure" by university representative Susan Worrall. The manuscript is accessible to the public without charge at the Edgbaston campus until October 25. The university library stated that these pages of the Islamic text had been unnoticed within their holdings for nearly a century. A visitor expressed awe at the find, pondering whether the Prophet Muhammad or his close companions might have handled the manuscript. Ms. Worrall, the director of special collections, celebrated the discovery as "fantastically exciting," highlighting the university's ownership of one of the oldest Quran fragments in existence. Birmingham's Muslim leaders have voiced their joy at the find, including Muhammad Afzal, chairman of Birmingham Central Mosque, who shared his sentiments after seeing the manuscript.

Following Alastair Cook's four-year tenure as captain, Joe Root, the Yorkshireman, has been appointed as his successor in the Test format. Both Root and his newly appointed vice-captain, Ben Stokes, emphasized the team's dual focus on winning and providing exciting cricket. Root, previously the vice-captain at 26 years old, will make his captaincy debut against South Africa at Lord's, starting July 7th. Stokes, the 25-year-old Durham all-rounder, now assumes the vice-captain role, highlighting the importance of Test cricket and his desire to reignite public interest. He affirmed his commitment to winning and insisted that his new role will not alter his character or playing style, as he remains dedicated to contributing comprehensively to the team's efforts.

Prime Minister Modi, addressing soldiers in Siachen – the high-altitude battleground between India and Pakistan – emphasized that their steadfast dedication ensures India's safety. Following this, he went to the flood-stricken Kashmir valley, where devastating floods had resulted in at least 281 deaths, inundated Srinagar, and displaced over a million people. This visit marks the second time an Indian Prime Minister has been to Siachen, the first being Manmohan Singh in 2005. Since India took control in 1984, the extreme weather on the glacier, with deployments reaching 22,000 ft (6,700m), has caused more soldier deaths than actual fighting. Modi's visit, which occurred during the Diwali festival, included meetings with top officials and aid workers to assess the ongoing relief efforts. The September floods in Indian-administered Kashmir damaged approximately 180,000 homes, leaving many still residing in relief camps.

A well-known nightclub in south-east London, the Elephant and Castle, has been opposing the construction of an apartment building opposite its location, fearing that future residents' noise complaints might lead to its shutdown. Southwark Council initially rejected the development, but Boris Johnson intervened. Liberal Democrat councillors who voted against the project were criticized for failing to reveal significant donations their party had received from the club during the planning session. These donations were not known to Labour councillors or the developer, Oakmayne, until the BBC revealed them. The council's legal counsel also cautioned the councillors that their failure to declare the donations could be illegal. Both Ministry of Sound and the Lib Dems maintain that their actions were ethical. In a letter to

If enacted, these legal revisions would represent the first instance of Japanese military involvement in overseas combat operations since the Second World War. Having already cleared Japan's House of Representatives, the legislation is anticipated to gain approval from the upper house. Although Japan's constitution renounces the use of force in settling international disputes, save for self-defense, a revised interpretation now permits "collective self-defense," enabling the use of force to defend allies facing attack. Police are controlling demonstrators in central Tokyo to reduce disturbances. Despite the rainy weather, tens of thousands of people have protested in the streets, calling for the preservation of their pacifist constitution and the prime minister's resignation. Despite the presence of police vehicles, the unusual display of public opposition in Japan indicates a limited likelihood of escalation. These predominantly citizen-organized demonstrations have persisted throughout the summer months.

On Sunday, she declared her intention to remain the Member of Parliament for Brighton Pavilion, with plans to increase her engagement in active politics. First elected in 2008, she became the Green Party's first sole leader for England and Wales, a change from their previous dual speaker leadership. She then broke ground as their first MP in the 2010 general election. She explained on Twitter that her resignation as leader was to allow a new leader to emerge. Elaborating on BBC Radio 4's Westminster Hour, she said that by not seeking re-election, she would open opportunities for others to rise, strengthen their position in the party, and potentially achieve electoral success. She highlighted the party's recent accomplishments, including securing their inaugural Westminster seat, gaining control of their first local council, and increasing their overall vote share in the latest election.

Corrie McKeague, a 23-year-old Royal Air Force gunner stationed at RAF Honington in Suffolk, disappeared on the morning of September 24 after spending the previous evening in Bury St Edmunds. His mother, Nicola Urquhart, described his disappearance as out of character, stating in a BBC interview with Victoria Derbyshire that he would never normally vanish without getting in touch. Urquhart also noted that McKeague, originally from Dunfermline, Fife, was known to accept rides from people he didn't know. CCTV last recorded him at 3:20 AM BST in Bury St Edmunds, walking alone while eating takeaway food. His mobile phone signal was tracked from Bury St Edmunds to Barton Mills that same day, with data indicating a 28-minute journey, consistent with the driving time between the two places; however, the phone's whereabouts remain unknown.

Regina Hungerford, a 56-year-old teacher, refuted allegations of striking a 17-year-old student wearing headphones in her Merthyr Tydfil College classroom. Despite her denial, a disciplinary board concluded that physical contact likely occurred, deeming her behavior "unacceptable." The Education Workforce Council suspended her on Thursday, stating that barring her from teaching was in the "public interest." Hungerford admitted to raising her voice and slamming a book on the desk of the "provocative and disruptive" teenager as he listened to rap music, but insisted she did not hit his head. Although cleared of criminal assault charges concerning the math lesson for students with learning disabilities, a disciplinary panel, after an appeal in November, determined she probably made physical contact with the student's head or hand, judging her actions "inappropriate."

Eric Morecambe acquired his Jensen Interceptor in 1968 and kept it at his residence until its 2014 sale to Silverstone Auctions. Subsequently, Silverstone Auctions commissioned Jensen experts Cropredy Bridge to overhaul the engine, brakes, and body. Morecambe, who passed away in 1984, was the only owner of the car, which he received directly from Jensen's West Bromwich factory on September 23, 1968. Silverstone Auctions, based in Hertfordshire Warwickshire, created a website detailing the car's history and restoration, featuring stories from Morecambe's chauffeur, Mike Fountain, who occasionally drove Eric and his wife Joan. Fountain recalled the car's two-seater design resulted in cramped conditions, often with Morecambe "screwed up in the back," but emphasized the Jensen was the comedian's preferred vehicle.

Following a Supreme Court decision, N. Srinivasan, the BCCI president whose ownership of an IPL team has made him a powerful figure in global cricket governance, has stepped aside temporarily. Despite being elected ICC chairman in February, scheduled to begin in July, he was succeeded by Sunil Gavaskar as interim BCCI president last month. This move was prompted by the Supreme Court's order for the BCCI to form a panel to investigate corruption allegations against Srinivasan and twelve others, including players, underscoring the court's concern about the seriousness of the accusations.

Belgian news sources reported that a silent, solemn march was led by individuals directly affected by the suicide bombings at the Brussels airport and metro that killed 32 people. Originally scheduled for the week following the March 22 attacks, the demonstration was delayed at the request of authorities due to security concerns. On Sunday, the march included victims' family members, paramedics, airport employees, and people of various faiths, all carrying flowers to honor the dead. The procession passed through Molenbeek, the neighborhood of many suspected Brussels and Paris attackers, and concluded at the temporary memorial near the city's stock exchange. According to AFP, march organizer Hassan Bousetta stated, "When defenseless civilians, our fellow citizens, are murdered in a cowardly attack, all citizens must rise up to show their solidarity and abhorrence."

UEFA is considering adding goal-line technology to their matches, possibly in conjunction with the current additional assistant referees stationed by each goal. Following discussions on Friday, a decision is expected in January. This technology, already used in the Premier League since the 2013-14 season and by FIFA at the 2014 World Cup, is viewed favorably by UEFA's general secretary, Gianni Infantino, who cited "logistical challenges" at a Paris press conference. Infantino noted the long-term review of the technology and suggested that if implemented for Euro 2016, it would also be used in the Champions League and Europa League the following season, complementing the existing five assistant referee system. While the final decision is set for January, the executive committee seems generally in favor of the change.

Domino's Pizza Enterprises, an Australian-based company with master franchise rights for Domino's in various nations, reported a 56.7% increase in net profit, reaching A$45.6 million, a significant jump from the previous year. The pizza giant attributed this considerable growth to its internal expansion strategies, demonstrating its ability to thrive despite worldwide economic challenges. After its second profit revision upwards since December, the company's share price experienced a surge of over 10% on Wednesday. Domino's also noted substantial growth in Japan, with 48 new stores in the latter half of the year, and affirmed that its Australian and New Zealand operations are poised to surpass their target of 50 new store launches.

England suffered a heartbreaking defeat against the West Indies, largely due to Carlos Brathwaite's incredible feat of hitting four successive sixes against Ben Stokes in the final over. Despite the loss, Cook praised Stokes' exceptional talent and character, predicting he would overcome this setback and achieve significant milestones, perhaps even a Test score of 250. Cook acknowledged Brathwaite's extraordinary hitting prowess, noting that while Stokes might rue his first ball, his subsequent delivery was not drastically off, yet still traveled a remarkable 94 meters. Visibly distressed, Cook admitted to BBC Essex that cricket rarely evokes such emotion in him. He lamented that the otherwise excellent tournament concluded on a sour note, with the final over unfolding unexpectedly. Cook's county team, Essex, is set to begin a new chapter under their new coach, Chris Silverwood, on Sunday.

Authorities suspect a man's death was caused by a heroin overdose, possibly intensified by the presence of the much stronger opioids fentanyl or carfentanyl. Police discovered him unconscious at a residence in Fitzwilliam, near Wakefield, on Sunday, and he subsequently died in a hospital. A 43-year-old man has been arrested regarding the incident. Det Ch Insp Stuart Spencer of West Yorkshire Police is cautioning heroin users, especially those buying drugs on the street, to exercise extreme caution regarding their drug use. This warning follows a string of fatal overdoses in Hull, Barnsley, Leeds, and Normanton, West Yorkshire, connected to "deadly batches" of heroin. Earlier, in March, Cleveland Police associated six fatalities in Stockton-on-Tees with a specific heroin batch.

Masai Graham's clever quip, "My dad suggested I register for a donor card, he's a man after my own heart," earned him the "Joke of the Fringe" title. A group of 10 judges chose the top jokes from the Edinburgh Fringe Festival, and the public then voted on a selection of finalists. Sponsored by the Dave TV channel, the award has been previously claimed by comedians like Tim Vine, Stewart Francis, and Zoe Lyon. Graham, from West Bromwich, who was a finalist in both 2014 and 2015, expressed his delight, stating, "It's an incredible honour to land Joke of the Fringe. Not bad for someone from West Brom!" Stuart Mitchell came in second with the joke: "Why is it old people say 'there's no place like home', yet when you put them in one..." The judges were required to watch around 60 comedy performances each.

Erika Murray, 31, was taken into custody Thursday night after a neighbor raised concerns about the welfare of children residing in her residence. Upon investigation, detectives discovered remains inside the property, which they characterized as being extremely dirty and infested with pests. Ms. Murray entered a not guilty plea to all charges on Friday, which included concealing a fetal death, intimidating a witness, and child endangerment. Her attorney, Keith Halpern, suggested a potential mental health issue, commenting after the court hearing that while people seek explanations in such cases, mental illness doesn't always offer straightforward solutions. According to Worcester district attorney spokesman Tim Connolly, police were initially dispatched to the Blackstone home following a report that a ten-year-old boy living there had asked a neighbor, "How do you get a baby to stop crying?"

Jack Whitley, Chelsea's goalkeeper from 1907 to 1914, represented the club in their inaugural top-flight season. Upon his death, he requested burial in Brompton Cemetery despite residing outside London. The Chelsea Supporters' Trust has launched a crowdfunding campaign to fund a gravestone for Whitley, as it's thought his widow lacked the means. Chelsea's official historian, Rick Glanvill, emphasized the significance of a headstone, stating it would be deeply meaningful. Glanvill, researching the links between the club and the cemetery, noted its proximity to the stadium and that, despite the burial of the club's original owner and a director there, something felt incomplete.

During the Sharjah match, 24-year-old all-rounder Ben Stokes injured his arm while diving to catch a shot, ultimately leaving the field with his arm in a sling. Stokes, fielding at backward square leg, attempted to catch Sarfraz Ahmed's shot off Samit Patel when the incident occurred. England teammate Stuart Broad told BBC Sport that it was immediately apparent Stokes was injured upon landing. Broad voiced his concern but highlighted the team's ability to adapt should Stokes be unable to play further. Visibly in pain following the fall, Stokes received medical attention and was seen departing the field with his shirt fashioned into a makeshift sling.

In April 2014, Boko Haram abducted 276 girls, with 21 regaining freedom through Red Cross negotiation in October. However, a BBC report exposed that their Christmas reunion in Chibok, despite being under government protection post-release, was overshadowed by restrictions. The girls were confined to a politician's residence, prohibited from going to their homes or celebrating Christmas church services with their families. While they were taken to a local official's home to meet their parents, they were still not allowed to return home. One distraught father lamented this felt like renewed captivity, expressing disbelief that his daughter was so close yet unable to come home and attend Christmas church services. Another parent described a soldier confiscating his phone when he attempted to photograph his daughter, stating security personnel intervened after he took a picture of them together.

Police have named Banjong Pongphon, the mayor of Padang Besar, as a primary suspect who wields significant power in the region where 26 bodies were unearthed from mass graves last week. Padang Besar is a sub-district in southern Songkhla province. According to the UN refugee agency, the first quarter of 2015 saw 25,000 migrants from Myanmar and Bangladesh journeying on smugglers' vessels, doubling the figure from the previous year. The UNHCR has stated that smuggler encampments nestled within the forests and plantations around Padang Besar serve as the principal destinations for these migrants. The autopsies to determine the cause of death of the bodies recovered from the Songkhla graves are still pending.

To highlight the impact of budget cuts on traditional policing, the police federation, representing 1,000 county officers, has launched a public campaign using bus and newspaper advertisements. They point out that Wiltshire Police has lost 153 officers since 2010. While Chief Constable Mike Veale acknowledges the impact of these cuts, he maintains the force's dedication to local policing. The federation's "Cuts Have Consequences" campaign underscores Wiltshire's position as having the fewest officers per capita in the UK, warning that this 16% workforce reduction results in slower response times, increased nighttime vulnerability to crime, and impunity for drink-drivers. With £17 million already cut from the budget and at least £10 million more expected, the federation, through chairman Mike White, emphasizes that personnel costs constitute 80% of the policing budget.

On January 24, 2015, Olney Rugby Club will host a charity rugby match honoring Edgar Mobbs, the celebrated England international and Northampton Saints captain. This event is a tribute to the England vs. Scotland match Mobbs arranged on January 30, 1915, as a recruitment drive for his World War One battalion. The commemorative match will feature a contest between players from the East Midlands and The 1st Battalion of the Yorkshire Regiment, as well as a game between Olney Ladies and the Army Women's XV. Mobbs, born in Northampton in 1882 and a former Olney player, led Northampton Rugby Football Club from 1907. After scoring a try against Australia in his 1909 debut, he won seven England caps and rose from private to battalion commander. He participated in major battles, was awarded the Distinguished Service Order, and received two mentions in Despatches before his death on July 31 during the battle of Passchendale.

A new report from a charity has revealed a stark imbalance: over half of the world's 21 million refugees are being sheltered by only ten countries, which collectively represent a mere 2.5% of global GDP. Salil Shetty of Amnesty International condemned richer countries, singling out the UK, for not taking in enough refugees. He noted that since 2011, the UK has resettled approximately 8,000 Syrian refugees, while the US has taken in a mere 12,000. According to UN figures, China, Russia, and Gulf nations have not resettled any Syrian refugees at all. In contrast, Jordan, with a GDP just 1.2% of the UK's, hosts nearly 655,000 Syrian refugees and more than 2.7 million refugees overall, making it the world's leading host nation, followed by Turkey (over 2.5 million), Pakistan (1.6 million), and Lebanon (over 1.5 million).

On Monday afternoon, CCTV captured a man emptying the contents of Jonathan Gwyer's food waste bin into his general waste bin outside his Whitstable residence. The incident prompted an apology from Serco, the waste management company, who deemed the actions of their agency employee "completely unacceptable." Gwyer, a resident of Colombia Avenue, expressed frustration, questioning the value of recycling and the need for waste segregation. While acknowledging the allure of a single bin system, he primarily faulted Serco, rather than the individual worker, recognizing the challenges of the job and noting a recent increase in rushed and less organized behavior among the workers. Serco responded with a statement reaffirming their commitment to recycling practices.

The Community Charge Debt bill sets a deadline to stop local councils from chasing unpaid poll tax. After the Scottish independence vote, larger voter rolls, resulting from increased registration, were used to locate people with outstanding poll tax debts. The Scottish government has pledged to compensate councils for this initiative. Scotland implemented the poll tax, or community charge, in 1989 under Margaret Thatcher's Conservative government, ahead of the rest of the UK, and it was repealed in 1993 after four years, replacing the old rates system. This unpopular tax triggered widespread public demonstrations. Scottish local authorities have witnessed a decrease in recovered poll tax arrears, falling under £350,000 in 2013-14, with some councils halting debt collection. Deputy First Minister John Swinney described the poll tax as a "hated levy" that inflicted suffering on Scottish communities and was widely considered an unworkable and universally unpopular tax.

Despite expressing a shared commitment to combatting extremism and strengthening the economy, hopes for a comprehensive agreement between Libya's rival leaders diminished after they released separate statements on Wednesday. The meetings in the United Arab Emirates this week between Fayez Sarraj, leader of the UN-recognized government, and Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army (LNA) and controller of eastern Libya, took place against a backdrop of Libyan instability that has persisted since the 2011 overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi. Haftar has resisted international attempts to resolve the conflict by refusing to recognize Sarraj's Government of National Accord (GNA) since its formation in 2015. According to a Reuters source with ties to the GNA leadership, the initial plan was to issue a joint statement, but the parties ultimately decided to release individual statements, both of which called for an end to Libya's political and economic turmoil.

In July 2014, a Nottinghamshire woman from Eastwood repeatedly contacted the police about Craig Hutsby, citing threats and violations of his bail conditions. Despite these reports, Hutsby raped her the next month. A subsequent investigation by the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) found that the rape could have been avoided if arrest forms had been processed promptly. Detective Superintendent Rachel Walker stated that officers faced misconduct hearings as a result. The IPCC found PC Sofi Essex guilty of misconduct for neglecting to prepare the mandatory "arrest package"—the paperwork needed to make an arrest—when instructed. The IPCC determined that this delay prevented the timely apprehension of Hutsby, allowing the rape to occur. Additionally, PC Joseph Lovelock was found guilty of misconduct by the IPCC for improperly completing a form related to the victim, which resulted in a failure to recognize her high-risk status and implement appropriate protective measures.

Before a crowd of 15,000 in Berlin, SKT1 of South Korea defeated their countrymen, the Koo Tigers, to claim the championship title and the $1 million reward (£650,000). SKT1 secured a 3-1 victory in the final, with the Koo Tigers being the sole team to win a game against them in the entire competition. After the victory, SKT1's Gyeong-hwan Jang commented, "We have consistently performed well against Koo due to frequent encounters. We observed minimal strategic adjustments from them throughout the year, allowing for accurate predictions." Jang, also known as Marin, received the most valuable player award for his critical contribution to SKT1's second championship win, particularly notable as only two players remained from their 2013 championship-winning roster.

Former Zimbabwe international Tatenda Taibu, 32, who played 28 Tests and 150 ODIs before his 2012 retirement, made an unexpected approach to Hightown Cricket Club. Hightown's publicity officer, Nick Gordon, initially thought it was a prank, stating, "I didn't believe it when he told me who he was." However, after verifying Taibu's identity through Zimbabwean cricket contacts, discussions progressed, leading Gordon to acknowledge, "It's a massive achievement for us." The former wicketkeeper-batsman is scheduled to debut for the Second Division team against Alder on April 24. Gordon told BBC Radio Merseyside that Taibu replied to the club's advertisement for an international player, emphasizing the surprising nature of the signing: "It's not every day that Hightown St Mary's signs a player of Tatenda's caliber. I was taken aback; it was very strange."

In a historic meeting, the first of its kind since diplomatic ties were normalized two decades prior, President Obama acknowledged the burgeoning US-Vietnam alliance, notwithstanding their contrasting political ideologies. Experts suggest this strengthened bond acts as a strategic check on China's expanding power. Coinciding with the Vietnam War's 40th anniversary, Obama acknowledged the complex history and ongoing political differences, while highlighting the development of a mutually advantageous and respectful rapport. Mr. Trong characterized the discussions as "cordial, constructive, positive, and frank," emphasizing their transformation from adversaries to allies and comprehensive partners, conveying hope for sustained advancement and extending an invitation for Obama to visit Vietnam.

Recognizing the serious danger al-Shabab presents, the official pointed to a recent video from the Somalia-based group encouraging attacks on shopping centers in the US, Canada, and the UK. He referenced al-Shabab's previous claim of responsibility for the 2013 Westgate mall attack in Nairobi, where 67 people died. Speaking to CNN, he described the threat as "a new phase" of terrorism, involving more attacks by "independent actors in their homelands." He emphasized the need to take any terrorist group's call for specific attacks seriously but clarified that he was not recommending people avoid the malls mentioned by the militants. The video showed a masked man with a British accent urging al-Shabab followers to attack "American or..." targets.

Following discussions with Irish Taoiseach Enda Kenny, the British Prime Minister characterized the UK and Ireland as "close friends." Kenny expressed his satisfaction with the increasingly strong ties between the two nations. Cameron is scheduled to attend a state banquet with the Queen and Duke of Edinburgh during their landmark four-day trip—the first by a British monarch since Ireland gained independence. Cameron emphasized that the Queen's visit highlights the potential for an even stronger relationship, founded on trade, investment, economic links, and joint opportunities for neighboring partners. He also recognized the Queen's "great understanding" of the complex shared past of the UK and Ireland. While Cameron and Kenny had previously met in Downing Street in April, this marks their initial encounter in Ireland since Kenny assumed the role of Taoiseach in March.

Spoof accounts, some using names like NASA and the Environmental Protection Agency, have emerged to challenge the president's views, particularly his dismissal of climate change as a hoax. For example, @RogueNASA, identifying itself as NASA's unofficial "Resistance" team, stresses its independence from the agency and government, while promising factual information presented with irony. Similarly, @ActualEPAFacts, a parallel EPA account contacted by BBC News, declared its intention to keep sharing factual data on climate change and scientific studies under the Trump administration. The operators, claiming to be three EPA employees, said they were motivated by a gag order restricting them from discussing their research publicly. News sources indicate that the Trump administration has attempted to curb public communication from certain government bodies, including the EPA, whose official Twitter account has been inactive since the day before Trump's inauguration.

Despite the Labour party's official pro-EU position, concerns have been raised that Jeremy Corbyn, a long-standing EU skeptic, needs to advocate for it with greater conviction. Anxious Labour MPs cautioned that a less passionate pro-EU effort from Corbyn could jeopardize the referendum's outcome. A spokesperson announced his plans to deliver a significant speech on the subject soon. While visiting Dagenham, Corbyn acknowledged the EU's imperfections requiring improvement, but stressed the significance of European solidarity within Labour's existing campaign. He affirmed Labour's focus on "social justice across Europe," highlighting the social chapter on workers' rights and the Working Time Directive, while also mentioning efforts to gain backing from socialist parties throughout Europe.
